title: Menopause and Hormone Therapy in Brisbane: A Modern, Evidence-Based Approach
html:
Understanding Menopause

Menopause is defined as the point at which a woman has not had a menstrual period for 12 consecutive months, marking the end of ovarian reproductive function. In Australia, the average age of natural menopause is 51 to 52 years. The transition leading up to menopause – perimenopause – can begin 4 to 10 years earlier and is often the period during which symptoms are most disruptive.

During perimenopause and menopause, the ovaries progressively reduce their production of oestrogen, progesterone, and testosterone. This hormonal shift affects virtually every system in the body and can produce a wide range of symptoms that vary considerably between women in their nature, severity, and duration.

Common Symptoms of Menopause

The symptoms of menopause extend well beyond the hot flushes that most people associate with the transition. They include:

Vasomotor symptoms – hot flushes and night sweats are the most recognised menopausal symptoms, affecting approximately 75% of women. They can range from mild and occasional to severe and disruptive, significantly impacting sleep and daily functioning.

Sleep disturbance – difficulty falling asleep, frequent waking, and non-restorative sleep are extremely common during perimenopause and menopause, often compounded by night sweats.

Mood and cognitive changes – anxiety, depression, irritability, poor concentration, and memory difficulties are frequently reported. Many women describe a sense of cognitive fog or emotional instability that is unfamiliar and distressing.

Genitourinary symptoms – vaginal dryness, reduced lubrication, discomfort during intercourse, and increased urinary frequency or urgency are common and often undertreated.

Sexual changes – reduced libido, difficulty with arousal, and changes in sexual satisfaction affect many women during and after menopause.

Musculoskeletal symptoms – joint aches, muscle stiffness, and reduced muscle mass are frequently reported and contribute to reduced physical capacity.

Metabolic changes – the hormonal shifts of menopause are associated with increased abdominal fat accumulation, changes in cholesterol profile, and increased cardiovascular risk.

Bone density loss – oestrogen plays a critical role in maintaining bone density. The accelerated bone loss that occurs in the years around menopause significantly increases the long-term risk of osteoporosis and fracture.

The Modern Evidence on Hormone Therapy

Hormone therapy (HT) – previously called hormone replacement therapy or HRT – has had a complicated history. The publication of the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) study in 2002 caused widespread alarm about the risks of HRT, leading to a dramatic decline in prescribing and leaving many women without effective treatment for debilitating symptoms.

In the years since, the WHI findings have been substantially reinterpreted. The study used older, synthetic hormones (conjugated equine oestrogen and medroxyprogesterone acetate) in older women (average age 63) who were well past the menopausal transition. The risks identified in that population do not apply to younger, recently menopausal women using modern hormone preparations.

The current consensus from leading menopause societies – including the Australasian Menopause Society, the British Menopause Society, and the North American Menopause Society – is that for healthy women under 60 who are within 10 years of menopause onset, the benefits of hormone therapy substantially outweigh the risks.

Modern Hormone Therapy Options

Contemporary hormone therapy has evolved significantly from the preparations used in the WHI study. Options now include:

Body-identical oestrogen – oestradiol preparations (patches, gels, sprays) that are chemically identical to the oestrogen produced by the human ovary. These are distinct from the synthetic conjugated equine oestrogens used in older studies and have a more favourable safety profile.

Micronised progesterone – body-identical progesterone (Prometrium, Utrogestan) that is structurally identical to naturally produced progesterone. Evidence suggests it has a more favourable cardiovascular and breast safety profile than older synthetic progestogens.

Testosterone – as discussed in our article on low testosterone in women, testosterone therapy is an important component of comprehensive menopause care, particularly for women experiencing low libido, fatigue, and cognitive changes.

Transdermal delivery – oestrogen delivered through the skin (patches, gels, sprays) does not pass through the liver before entering the circulation, avoiding the increased clotting risk associated with oral oestrogen preparations.

A Comprehensive Approach to Menopause at Australian Longevity Clinic

At Australian Longevity Clinic, we take a comprehensive, individualised approach to menopause care that goes beyond simply prescribing hormones. Our assessment includes:

Full hormonal panel – measuring oestradiol, progesterone, testosterone, FSH, LH, SHBG, and thyroid function to establish a complete picture of your hormonal status.

Metabolic assessment – including fasting glucose, insulin, lipid profile, and inflammatory markers to assess cardiovascular and metabolic risk.

Bone density assessment – for women at increased osteoporosis risk, we can arrange DEXA scanning and provide targeted bone health support.

Individualised treatment planning – hormone therapy is tailored to your specific symptom profile, health history, risk factors, and personal preferences. We discuss all options – including non-hormonal approaches – and support you in making an informed decision.

Peptide support – for women seeking additional support beyond hormones, peptide therapies including BPC-157 (gut health), GHK-Cu (skin and tissue repair), and Epitalon (cellular longevity and sleep) can complement hormone therapy as part of a comprehensive longevity program.

Lifestyle medicine – nutrition, resistance training, sleep optimisation, and stress management are integral to our approach and are addressed alongside any hormonal treatment.

Who Is Hormone Therapy Suitable For?

Hormone therapy is appropriate for most healthy women experiencing menopausal symptoms who are under 60 and within 10 years of their last menstrual period. It is particularly beneficial for women with:

  • Moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes, night sweats)
  • Significant sleep disturbance, mood changes, or cognitive symptoms
  • Genitourinary symptoms affecting quality of life
  • Premature or surgical menopause
  • Increased osteoporosis risk

Hormone therapy requires careful consideration in women with a personal history of oestrogen-sensitive breast cancer, unexplained vaginal bleeding, active liver disease, or certain clotting disorders. A thorough medical assessment is essential.
